expectations.evidence: Baseline gives 8 numbered items (Language list, Experience list, Process narration, Quality adjective stack, Follow best practices, Test mentally, Always aim to be helpful, Alternatives instruction). This exceeds the 3–5 range, indicating a lack of prioritization — surfacing everything rather than identifying the highest-impact changes.

expectations.text: At least one recommendation explains WHY the change saves tokens (not just what to change)
expectations.evidence: Item 1: '"Expert software engineer" implies all of it.' Item 6: 'Unmeasurable, no real effect.' These provide causal reasoning.

expectations.text: Response includes a token savings estimate (percentage or count)
expectations.evidence: 'Suggested lean version (~60 tokens, ~75% reduction)' and 'Token savings: ~160-175 tokens per call. At 100k calls/month, that is 16-17 million tokens saved.'

expectations.text: Response opens with a one-sentence diagnosis of the prompt's main inefficiency
expectations.evidence: Starts with 'Original prompt: ~175 words / ~220-240 tokens' then 'What to cut:' — this is a data point and a section header, not a diagnosis sentence.

expectations.text: Response specifically identifies the language enumeration list as a token optimization opportunity
expectations.evidence: Item 1: 'Language list — "Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Rust, Java, C++, and many other programming languages" is unnecessary. "Expert software engineer" implies all of it.'

eval_feedback.overall: The recommendation-count assertion is a strong discriminator here — the baseline's list of 8 items vs the skill's 5 prioritized recommendations is a meaningful quality difference the assertion catches.
